summary: Chinese says ‘where to’ with the verb itself: 去 ‘go (there)’, 来 ‘come (here)’, 回 ‘go back’, 进 ‘enter’, 到 ‘arrive’ take the place as their object — 我去学校 ‘I go to school’, no word for ‘to’ and no case. ‘Where from’ is 从 + place before the verb: 他从北京来. A whole trip is 从 A 到 B: 从我家到学校. How you travel is a small verb phrase BEFORE the main verb: 坐 + vehicle you ride in (坐公共汽车去 ‘go by bus’), 骑 + what you sit astride (骑自行车去 ‘go by bike’), 开车 ‘drive’, 走路 ‘on foot’. After a verb of movement, 来 / 去 show the direction seen from the speaker: 进来 ‘come in’, 进去 ‘go in’, 回来 ‘come back’, 出去 ‘go out’. The order is always: who – (when) – from where / how – movement verb – where to.

blocks.title: German zu, nach, in — Chinese: nothing
blocks.text: German ich gehe in die Schule / zur Schule / nach Hause: the preposition and the case depend on the place. Chinese has none of this: 去学校, 去超市, 回家, 到北京 — the movement verb carries the ‘to’.

blocks.title: The vehicle comes BEFORE the main verb
blocks.text: 我坐火车去北京 ‘I go to Beijing by train’. Put the other way round, 我去北京坐火车 means ‘I go to Beijing to take a train’ — the second verb is the purpose.

blocks.title: 回家, not *去家
blocks.text: Going to your own home is 回家 ‘return home’. 去 + home is only for someone else’s: 去我朋友家, 去奶奶家.

items.title: 离开 + place — leave (a place)
points: 他离开了北京。 He left Beijing.
The place is the object; no 从.

items.title: 出 / 出去 — go out
points: 他出去了。 He has gone out.

blocks.title: German gehen / fahren — Chinese 去 for both
blocks.text: German must choose gehen (on foot) or fahren (by vehicle); Hebrew הָלַךְ / נָסַע makes the same split. Chinese uses 去 for every trip and adds HOW only if it matters: 走路去, 坐车去, 开车去.

blocks.title: Asking
blocks.text: 你去哪里？ ‘where are you going?’ · 你从哪里来？ ‘where are you coming from?’ · 你怎么去？ ‘how are you getting there?’ — 坐公共汽车。

askYourself: Is the movement towards me (or the listener) → 来, or away → 去? Going back → 回 (+ place) / 回来 / 回去.
Do I name the goal? → put it right after the verb: 去学校, 回家, 到北京 — no word for ‘to’.
Is it my own home? → 回家, never *去家.
Do I name the starting point? → 从 + place BEFORE the verb: 从北京来.
A whole stretch? → 从 A 到 B.
How do I travel? → 坐 / 骑 / 开 + vehicle, or 走路 — before the movement verb.
Leaving a place? → 离开 + place; just leaving → 走; going out → 出去.
Into / out of / back, seen from where I stand? → verb + 来 (towards me) or 去 (away).
Did I put the vehicle or the 从-phrase at the end? → move it before the verb.
steps: From where (从 …) and how (坐 / 骑 / 开 / 走路).

traps: *我去到学校 / *我去在学校 → 我去学校.
*我来从北京 → 我从北京来.
*我去学校坐公共汽车 (= I go to school to take the bus) → 我坐公共汽车去学校.
*我坐自行车 → 我骑自行车.
*走公共汽车 → 坐公共汽车.
*我从北京离开 (word by word from ‘leave from’) → 我离开北京.
来 is not only ‘towards the speaker’: answering someone who calls you, ‘I’m coming!’ is 来了！

quiz.why: How you travel comes before the movement verb; the other order means ‘to take the bus’ as the purpose.
从 + place stands before the verb.

quiz.q: ‘I ride my bike to the park.’
quiz.why: 骑 for what you sit astride.

quiz.q: Someone knocks; you are inside. You say …
quiz.why: Come in (towards me): 请进 / 请进来; 进去 would be ‘go in (there)’.
The place is the object of 离开.

quiz.q: Which measure word for a plane?
quiz.why: 一架飞机; 辆 is for wheeled vehicles, 条 for boats (and streets, fish).

notes.text: Greek πάω στο σχολείο needs σε for the goal and puts the means after it (με το λεωφορείο); Chinese puts the goal right after the verb with no ‘to’ (去学校) and the means before the verb (坐公共汽车去学校).

Russian chooses the verb by means — идти on foot, ехать by vehicle — and needs в / на for the goal (иду в школу). Chinese uses 去 for both, adds 走路 / 坐车 before it, and the goal follows 去 with no preposition.
Spanish ir a la escuela needs a; Chinese 去学校 needs nothing. The means comes after in Spanish (en autobús), before in Chinese (坐公共汽车去).

English go to school / come from Beijing / by bus put ‘to’, ‘from’ and the means after the verb; Chinese puts 从 + place and the means before the verb and the goal right after it, with no ‘to’: 我从家坐公共汽车去学校.
French aller à l’école / venir de Pékin / en bus puts everything after the verb; Chinese: 从北京来, 坐公共汽车去, 去学校 — source and means before the verb, goal after it, no ‘to’.
German splits gehen / fahren by means and zu / nach / in by goal; Chinese 去 does all of it, adds the means before it, and needs no preposition for the goal.
Hindi often needs no postposition for a destination either (मैं स्कूल जाता हूँ ‘I go to school’) — like 去学校 — but puts it before the verb; Chinese after it. से ‘from’ ~ 从, also before the verb.
Spoken Persian often needs no preposition for the goal (madrese miram ‘I go to school’) — like 去学校 — but puts it before the verb; Chinese after it.
Marathi marks the goal with an ending and puts it before the verb (मी शाळेत जातो ‘I go to school’); Chinese puts the bare goal after 去: 我去学校.
Arabic dhahabtu ilā l-madrasa needs ilā ‘to’ after the verb and bi- for the means; Chinese needs no ‘to’ and puts the means before the verb: 坐公共汽车去学校.
Hebrew splits halakh (on foot) and nasa (by vehicle), as German does; Chinese uses 去 for every trip, with the means before it (走路去, 坐车去).
Turkish marks the goal with -e / -a before the verb (okula gidiyorum) and the means with -le (otobüsle); Chinese puts the goal after the verb, unmarked (去学校), and the means before it (坐公共汽车).
Japanese 学校に行く puts the goal before the verb with に and the means with で (バスで); Chinese: 坐公共汽车去学校 — means first, then 去, then the goal without a particle.
Korean 학교에 가요 puts the goal before the verb with 에 and the means with 로 (버스로); Chinese: 坐公共汽车去学校 — the means before, the goal after 去.
Finnish marks the goal by case (kouluun ‘to school’) and the means with -lla (bussilla); Chinese has no case: 坐公共汽车去学校.

Hungarian preverbs (bemegy ‘goes in’, kijön ‘comes out’) show direction together with the verb, much like Chinese 进去, 出来; the goal takes a case ending (iskolába), while the Chinese goal stands bare after 去.
Swahili ninaenda shuleni ‘I go to school’ marks the goal with -ni and puts the means after (kwa basi); Chinese: 坐公共汽车去学校.
Luganda marks the goal with a place word after the verb; Chinese puts the bare goal right after 去 and the means before the verb.
Vietnamese đi Hà Nội also takes the goal right after the verb with no ‘to’ — like 去北京 — but puts the means after it (đi bằng xe buýt); Chinese puts the means first: 坐公共汽车去.
Inuktitut marks goal and source with case endings on the noun (-mut ‘to’, -mit ‘from’); Chinese uses the verb itself for the goal (去学校) and 从 before the verb for the source.

seeAlso.note: German picks the verb by the means (gehen on foot, fahren by vehicle, fliegen) and the preposition and case by the place (in die Schule, zur Arbeit, nach Hause, mit dem Bus); Chinese uses 去 for every trip, puts 坐 / 骑 / 开 + vehicle before it and needs no preposition at all.

Hebrew, like German, separates הָלַךְ (go on foot) from נָסַע (go by vehicle) and marks the goal with לְ־ / אֶל and the vehicle with בְּ־ (בָּאוֹטוֹבּוּס); Chinese marks neither — the vehicle is a verb phrase (坐公共汽车) before 去.
Arabic says ‘go to’ with ذَهَبَ إِلَى (+ genitive), ‘from’ with مِنْ and the vehicle with بِ (بِالسَّيَّارَةِ ‘by car’); Chinese has 从 before the verb and nothing at all for ‘to’ and ‘by’.
从 and 到 are the coverbs of S11; here they frame a whole trip: 从 A 到 B.
